periods.activity_title: Changes I Have Noticed — Timescales of Change
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us — Students think about and write changes noticed in themselves, friends, school, and environment since Grades 3 and 4 (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening story of Saba and Aparna meeting after a year and noticing changes in each other. Students share aloud one change they have noticed in themselves or a friend over the past year, building a warm class conversation about change as something constant in our lives.

Students open Textbook p. 147 and respond in writing to the prompt about changes in themselves, friends, school, and environment since Grades 3 and 4. They write freely for a generous stretch, drawing on personal memory.

The class discusses what students wrote. The teacher guides them to sort changes into rough groupings by how long they take — changes over many years, changes within a few years, changes every year, changes in minutes or seconds — using examples from students' own writing (Textbook p. 149).

Students write one example of their own for each timescale grouping in their notebooks. The teacher invites two or three students to share, drawing out the idea that change is constant but moves at very different paces.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify observed changes in their environment by the timescale over which those changes occur.
periods.section_context: Changes in self, friends, school, and environment since Grades 3–4; changes over years, within years, yearly repeating changes, changes in minutes or seconds; growing taller, leaves falling and regrowing, sky changing colour.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Is any change you named happening for the first time ever, or does it happen again and again?' This surfaces the idea of repeating versus one-time change, which the class will keep returning to as they explore seasons. If students mention traditional or family-based observations — a tree that flowers every year, a river that swells in a particular period — invite those into the sorting, as they carry real ecological knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Long, Short, and Repeating — Writing the Timescale of Change
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us — Students name something that changes over years, within years, every year, and within minutes or seconds (p. 149)

time_bands.activity: The teacher puts four headings on the board: 'Takes Many Years', 'Within a Few Years', 'Every Year Again and Again', 'Minutes or Seconds'. The class quickly recalls examples from the previous unit's conversation to populate each column — one or two entries per column, entirely from students' own suggestions.

Students work individually. They open Textbook p. 149 and respond to the four prompts — one example each for something that changes over many years, within a few years, every year, and within minutes or seconds. They are encouraged to go beyond the textbook's examples and draw on what they see in their own neighbourhood, home, or school garden.

Students pair up and share their four examples. Pairs look for one change they both listed and one change only one of them noticed, then share their 'only one of us noticed' example with the class. The teacher lists a range of these on the board, celebrating the diversity of observations.
The teacher closes by asking: 'Which of these changes happens again and again in a pattern?' — a brief oral exit that plants the idea of rhythmic, repeating change.

periods.implied_lo: Students can generate and compare examples of change across different timescales and recognise which changes follow a repeating pattern.
periods.section_context: Something that takes many years to change; something that changes within a few years; changes that happen every year repeatedly; changes in minutes or seconds; students' own local and environmental examples.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to name changes they have personally observed — a tree outside their home, the colour of a pond across seasons, a grandparent's hair — rather than textbook-only answers. Ask: 'When something changes again and again on a schedule, what do we call that?' Let students attempt an answer before offering the word 'pattern' or 'rhythm'.

periods.activity_title: Day and Night Role-Play — Earth Rotates, Sun Stays
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night) — Students enact the Sun–Earth rotation role-play and torch-and-globe demonstration to experience day and night (p. 150)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure showing Earth's rotation and day/night sides (p. 150)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks the class: 'When you wake up in the morning, has the Sun moved, or has something else changed?' Students share ideas freely. The teacher notes that the class will find out by doing, not just by reading.

Students open Textbook p. 150. Two volunteers are chosen — one is the 'Sun' (standing still at the centre), one is the 'Earth' (standing at a distance and slowly rotating on the spot). As the Earth-student faces the Sun they say 'day, day, day'; when they turn away they say 'night, night, night'. Three or four pairs of students take turns so the whole class experiences the sensation of rotating.

The torch-and-globe demonstration follows. The teacher darkens the room as much as possible, shines the torch (Sun) onto the globe, and slowly rotates the globe. Students observe which parts of the globe are lit and which are in shadow. The class identifies where India is on the globe and watches it move into and out of the light.

Students draw a quick diagram in their notebooks: globe, torch beam, a lit half labelled 'day' and a dark half labelled 'night', with an arrow showing the direction of rotation. They write one sentence: 'Day and night happen because ___.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a physical model to explain how the rotation of an object around its own axis produces alternating day and night.
periods.section_context: Earth's rotation on its axis; Sun standing fixed; day and night sides of Earth; torch-and-globe model; globe features (seas, oceans covering three-fourths of Earth); India's position on the globe.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After the role-play, ask the Earth-student: 'Did you move in a circle around the Sun, or did you spin in one place?' — this distinction between rotation and revolution is important and often confused. When the globe is lit, ask: 'Which part of India is in day right now? What might people there be doing?' Keep the demonstration unhurried so every student can watch the shadow line move.

periods.activity_title: Which Countries Have Night When India Has Day?
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night) — Students study the globe and write which countries have night when India has daytime (p. 151)
periods.visual_aids: Globe used as primary observation tool; Textbook p. 151 task reference

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly re-runs the torch-and-globe setup from the previous unit's work. She positions the torch so that India is in full daylight, then asks students to look at the globe carefully and name what they observe on the opposite side.

Students open Textbook p. 151 and work on the Find Out task: studying the globe with the torch held steady on India, they identify countries that fall in the shadow (night) side and write them in the space provided. The teacher circulates, prompting students to name continents first, then specific countries they can read from the globe.

Students share their findings in a class discussion. The teacher writes the class's collective list on the board. Together they notice the pattern: countries roughly opposite India on the globe have night when India has day. Students add any countries to their own list that they missed.

Students write a short summary in their notebooks: 'When India has daytime, countries like ___, ___, and ___ have night, because ___.' The teacher invites two or three students to read their summary aloud, affirming scientific language about rotation and the lit/shadow sides of Earth.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a physical model of Earth to observe and record which regions experience day and night simultaneously, connecting this to Earth's rotation.
periods.section_context: Globe observation with torch as Sun; India's daytime position; countries/continents on the night side simultaneously; Earth's rotation and the lit/shadow divide.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'How would you explain to a younger student why it is night in some countries right now while we are in school?' This pushes students toward articulating the rotation explanation in their own words. If a student mentions time zones or different sunrise times in India, affirm the observation and connect it to the same rotation principle without requiring technical vocabulary.

periods.activity_title: Seasons' Chart — Building the Wall Chart from Observations
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons) — Classroom Activity Steps 1 and 2: prepare the large wall chart and fill it from journal observations shared across the class (p. 152)
materials: Large chart paper or newspaper sheets taped together
Students' personal observation notes or memories
periods.visual_aids: Wall chart grid drawn by the class (columns: April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March; rows: plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, human activities)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the Seasons' Chart activity from Textbook p. 152. Together the class draws the large wall chart grid on chart paper: four time-period columns and five theme rows. Column and row labels are added in large, legible writing with student volunteers doing the lettering.

The class works together to fill the chart. The teacher calls out one cell at a time — e.g., 'Plant life in April–June' — and students call out observations from their own experience and memory. The teacher (or a student scribe) writes brief notes in each cell. Every student contributes at least one observation. The teacher encourages observations of traditional or locally known signs — a tree that signals the rains, a bird that appears in a certain season — alongside the textbook's examples.
Students look at the completed chart and notice: which theme row has the most variety across time periods? Which time period seems to bring the most changes? They share observations aloud.
The teacher asks: 'Do you notice that many of these changes happen every year at roughly the same time?' — a brief oral pause that plants the idea of seasonality.

periods.implied_lo: Students can organise and record observations of environmental changes across themes and time periods to reveal patterns in a year-long cycle.
periods.section_context: Wall chart with four time periods (April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March) and five themes (plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, human activities); class-shared observations filling the grid; discovery of repeating annual patterns.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students have a seasons journal or nature diary from earlier in the year, invite them to use it; if not, their memories work equally well — the chart can be built entirely from lived experience. Ask about traditional ecological signs students have heard from family members: 'Has anyone been told by a grandparent or elder that a certain bird or plant signals a coming change in weather?' These observations belong on the chart.

periods.activity_title: Seasons' Chart — Theme Posters and Time-Period Stories
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons) — Classroom Activity Steps 3 and 4: form theme groups to make posters and regroup by time period to write short stories linking nature to human life (p. 152)
periods.visual_aids: The wall chart built in the preceding unit, displayed on the classroom wall

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly orients the class to the wall chart (Textbook p. 152, Steps 3 and 4). Five theme groups are formed quickly: plant life, birds and animals, air/heat/light, water and water bodies, human activities.

Each theme group takes a sheet of chart paper and creates a poster showing how their theme changed across all four time periods of the year, drawing from the wall chart data. They use drawings, labels, and colour. Groups are encouraged to include local examples — a crop or bird familiar to their region — alongside generic ones.

Groups dissolve and four new time-period groups form (April–June, July–September, October–December, January–March). Each group reads across all five theme rows for their time period from the wall chart and together writes a short story — five to eight sentences — that weaves nature changes and human life together for that time of year.
One member of each time-period group reads their story aloud. The class listens for how nature and people's lives are connected across the year.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations of seasonal environmental change through a creative mode — poster or written story — connecting natural patterns to human activities.
periods.section_context: Five-theme posters showing change across four time periods; short stories linking nature changes to human life for each of the four time periods; the wall chart data as the source for both creative products.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups before they write their stories: 'What do the people in your region do during this time of year that is connected to what nature is doing?' This keeps the human–nature link explicit. If a group mentions the koel bird's call or ants carrying eggs, acknowledge these as examples of traditional ecological knowledge and invite the class to discuss what these signs tell people about what is coming.

periods.activity_title: India's Six Seasons — Names, Sanskrit Ritu, and Regional Months
periods.section_ref: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
periods.textbook_anchor: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons) — Students fill in the months for India's six seasons in their region using the Sanskrit Ritu names (p. 152)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook table of India's six seasons with Sanskrit Ritu names

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'How many seasons does your family talk about? What do you call them at home?' Students share season names in their own languages. The teacher writes these on the board alongside the six Sanskrit Ritu names from the textbook: Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, Shishir.

Students open the textbook to the seasons table and fill in the months for each of the six seasons as they apply in their own region. The teacher invites students from different regional backgrounds to share their months — for example, when does Grishma (summer) peak? When does Varsha (monsoon) start? The class discovers that the same season begins at different months in different parts of India.

A whole-class discussion follows: Why might Hemant begin earlier in the north than in the south? What clues in nature tell people a new season is starting — not the calendar, but what they see, hear, smell, or feel? Students draw on the wall chart data and their own experience.
Students write three sentences in their notebooks: the name of the season they are currently in, its Sanskrit Ritu name, and one nature sign that tells them this season has arrived.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify India's seasonal cycle, name the seasons in their regional and classical traditions, and explain how the same season varies across different regions.
periods.section_context: India's six seasons with Sanskrit Ritu names (Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, Shishir); student-filled months table for their own region; regional variation in season onset; nature signs of season change.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'If you had to tell someone from another country when Vasanta (spring) begins in your town, would you give them a date or describe what they would see and hear?' This question surfaces the distinction between calendar-based and nature-based season knowledge. If students mention the koel bird or specific flowering trees as season signals, draw these out — they represent the same kind of knowledge as the Odisha example in the textbook.

periods.activity_title: Seasons, Crops, and Festivals — Connecting Nature to Cultural Life
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Seasons — Students name summer and winter crops in their region and match festivals to seasons (p. 157)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook table of festivals and their associated seasons; crops table

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a question: 'Does your family grow any food, or do you know what is available in the market in summer versus winter?' Students share what they know about seasonal produce and crops. The teacher notes that different crops need different seasons — some need cold, some heat, some rain.

Students open Textbook p. 157 and work on the crop-naming task: filling in summer and winter crops known in their region, with the teacher and classmates as resources. The class pools responses — the teacher lists crops on the board and asks which season each belongs to and why (what does that crop need — warmth, rain, cool nights?).

The class moves to festivals. The teacher asks: 'Which festivals do you celebrate, and what season do they fall in?' Students share and the teacher matches their answers to the textbook's festival–season pairings: Pongal and Makar Sankranti (winter), Holi (spring), Diwali (autumn), Baisakhi, Gudi Padwa, Vishu, Rongali Bihu (new year/harvest). Students note these in their textbook or notebook.

The teacher asks: 'Why do you think so many festivals happen right around harvest time?' Students discuss briefly. The teacher closes by drawing the link: seasons shape what grows, what is harvested, and what people celebrate.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between seasonal cycles and cultural practices — crops grown, festivals celebrated, and songs sung — in their own region.
periods.section_context: Summer and winter crops in students' regions; seasonal conditions needed by different crops; Pongal/Makar Sankranti (winter), Holi (spring), Diwali (autumn), Baisakhi/Gudi Padwa/Vishu/Rongali Bihu (new year/harvest); songs associated with seasons.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to name a festival not in the textbook's list that their family celebrates and identify which season it falls in — this surfaces regional diversity and validates students' cultural knowledge. If any student mentions ants carrying eggs before rain or other traditional ecological signs, connect this to the idea that communities developed ways of reading nature's calendar long before written calendars existed.

periods.activity_title: Why Winter in Kerala Differs from Kashmir — Regional Seasons Discussion
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Seasons — Students discuss why winter in Kerala differs from Kashmir valley and why monsoon in Assam differs from Rajasthan (p. 157)
periods.visual_aids: Political map of India (from classroom or textbook) showing location of Kerala, Kashmir, Assam, Rajasthan

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the Textbook p. 157 discuss question aloud: 'Winter in Kerala is different from winter in Kashmir valley. Monsoon in Assam is different from Rajasthan. Why do you think it is so?' Students think quietly for a moment, then share initial ideas with a partner.

The class discusses the two contrasts using the political map of India to locate the four regions. The teacher guides students to think about what is different about these places: how far north or south they are, how close to the sea, whether surrounded by mountains. Students are encouraged to draw on anything they know about weather in their own region or from travel and family stories.

Students write their own response to the two-part question in their notebooks — why the same season feels different in different parts of India — using the discussion as a scaffold. They also write a response to the reflection prompt from Textbook p. 157: 'Would you prefer one season to continue throughout the year? Give your reasons.'

Three or four students share their 'one season all year' reflections. The class listens and considers: whose life would benefit and whose would suffer if one season never ended? The teacher closes by drawing attention to how seasonal diversity across India supports the country's varied crops, cultures, and celebrations.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how geographical differences across regions produce variation in the experience of the same season, and can reflect on the value of seasonal diversity.
periods.section_context: Winter in Kerala versus Kashmir valley; monsoon in Assam versus Rajasthan; geographical reasons for seasonal variation (latitude, proximity to sea, mountains); student preference for a single season and reasoning; value of seasonal diversity for crops, culture, and life.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would happen to rice farming if there were no monsoon in Assam? What would happen to apple orchards in Kashmir if winters stopped being cold?' These concrete consequences help students see seasonal variation not just as climate fact but as something that shapes livelihoods and food. If students raise concerns about unusual seasons or unpredictable weather they have noticed, treat these as genuine observations worth taking seriously.

periods.activity_title: My Seasons — Local Names, Season Table, and Comparative Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Celebrating Seasons — Let us reflect: students write local season names, fill the season–food–clothes–festival–nature table, and make a comparative drawing of three seasons (p. 159–160)
materials: Drawing paper or the back of a notebook page

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 159 and find the local names task. They write the names of all six seasons (Spring, Summer, Monsoon, Autumn, Pre-winter, Winter) as they are called in their region and in their home language. The teacher invites two or three students to share — the class discovers that the same season carries many names across India.

Students move to Textbook p. 160 and fill the season table: for each of the six seasons they write the food they eat, clothes they wear, festivals they celebrate, and what nature looks like around them. They work individually but may quietly ask a neighbour. The teacher circulates and encourages specificity — a named dish, a named garment, a named festival.

Students take a fresh page and make the comparative drawing task from Textbook p. 160: three panels side by side showing Summer, Monsoon, and Winter as they look in their own locality. They label each panel and add at least two details in each (a plant, an activity, the sky, clothing, water body, or a festival element).

Students share their drawings with the person beside them and describe one detail that is different between their two drawings — reflecting the reality that even within the same class, students' seasonal experiences may differ by family background, location, or community.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present their personal and regional experience of seasons through multiple creative modes — written local names, a completed observation table, and a comparative drawing.
periods.section_context: Local language names for six seasons; season table (food eaten, clothes worn, festivals celebrated, nature observed) for each of Spring, Summer, Monsoon, Autumn, Pre-winter, Winter; comparative drawing of Summer, Monsoon, and Winter as experienced in students' own locality.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Assure students that there is no single correct answer for local season names, foods, or festivals — regional and family differences are exactly what this task is designed to capture. Ask: 'Did any of your season details surprise your neighbour? What does that tell us about how differently people experience the same time of year?' If a student's table includes a food or festival the class is unfamiliar with, invite a brief explanation — this is the diversity the chapter is celebrating.

assessment_items.question_text: Saba notices that a mango tree near her house flowers every year around the same time and then bears fruit. Which timescale of change does this best represent?

options.label: A
options.text: A change that happened only once and will not happen again

options.label: B
options.text: A change that happens every year in a repeating pattern

options.label: C
options.text: A change that happens within just a few seconds

options.label: D
options.text: A change that takes many years to happen

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. The mango tree's yearly flowering and fruiting is the defining example of a repeating annual pattern discussed in the 'Changes Around Us' section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify observed changes in their environment by the timescale over which those changes occur.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses a long-term one-time change (like a mountain eroding) with a yearly recurring cycle — they have not distinguished timescale types.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has associated 'tree change' with rapid, moment-to-moment change rather than recognising the annual pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not recognise that natural cycles repeat — they may believe all change is directional and non-reversible.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'Every morning the Sun rises in the east. This means the Sun must be moving around the Earth each day.' Do you agree? Write two or three sentences explaining what actually causes morning and night, using what you know about the Earth.
expected_elements: States that the Earth rotates on its own axis, not the Sun moving around Earth.
Explains that as Earth rotates, the part facing the Sun experiences day and the part facing away experiences night.
Uses the idea of a fixed Sun and a spinning Earth to correct the student's statement.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response names Earth's rotation, distinguishes the lit and dark sides, and explicitly corrects the misconception. Award full credit for responses that capture all three elements in the student's own words.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a physical model to explain how the rotation of an object around its own axis produces alternating day and night.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

expected_elements: States that the Earth rotates on its own axis, not the Sun moving around Earth.
Explains that as Earth rotates, the part facing the Sun experiences day and the part facing away experiences night.
Uses the idea of a fixed Sun and a spinning Earth to correct the student's statement.

assessment_items.question_text: When a torch is shone on a globe so that India is in the light, which part of the globe will be in darkness?

options.label: A
options.text: The part of the globe closest to the torch

options.label: B
options.text: The part of the globe on the opposite side from the torch's light

options.label: C
options.text: The part of the globe that is tilted sideways

options.label: D
options.text: The top of the globe (the North Pole)

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. This item directly tests the observation made during the torch-and-globe activity: the side opposite the light source is in shadow.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Day (Day and Night)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a physical model of Earth to observe and record which regions experience day and night simultaneously, connecting this to Earth's rotation.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the relationship — they think proximity to the light source means darkness, a confusion about how shadows are cast.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the axis orientation with the lit/shadow divide, suggesting they did not clearly observe how the shadow falls on the globe.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing the tilt of Earth's axis (a separate concept) with the day/night shadow — conflating two ideas from the same chapter.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the Seasons' Chart your class built. Choose any one theme row (for example, 'water and water bodies' or 'plant life'). Describe two changes you noticed in that theme across two different time periods of the year, and explain what pattern you can see.
expected_elements: Names a specific theme row from the chart.
Describes a distinct change in that theme for two different time periods (e.g., rivers full in July–September, rivers low in April–June).
States that the pattern repeats every year at roughly the same time, connecting it to the idea of seasons.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any theme row and any pair of time periods. Regional variation in observations is expected and correct — a student from Rajasthan and a student from Assam may describe very different changes for the 'water and water bodies' row, and both are valid. Award credit for a clear statement of the repeating pattern.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can organise and record observations of environmental changes across themes and time periods to reveal patterns in a year-long cycle.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Names a specific theme row from the chart.
Describes a distinct change in that theme for two different time periods (e.g., rivers full in July–September, rivers low in April–June).
States that the pattern repeats every year at roughly the same time, connecting it to the idea of seasons.

assessment_items.task: Choose one time period from the year (April–June, July–September, October–December, or January–March). Draw a picture showing what nature looks like during that time period AND what people in your area are doing because of those nature changes. Write two sentences below your drawing explaining the connection.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My time period: ___
What nature looks like: (draw here)
What people are doing: (add to the drawing)
My two sentences:
1. During this time, nature ___.
2. Because of this, people in my area ___.
format_of_output: A labelled drawing showing nature and human activity for one time period
Two written sentences connecting the nature change to human activity
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any of the four time periods. The drawing and sentences should show a clear connection between a nature change and a human activity — this is the core of the Seasons' Chart Step 4 work. Regional variation is expected and all regionally accurate responses are correct.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations of seasonal environmental change through a creative mode — poster or written story — connecting natural patterns to human activities.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can visually and verbally represent the relationship between seasonal environmental change and human activity for a specific time period, demonstrating that they have synthesised the Seasons' Chart observations into a meaningful nature–human connection.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold gives students a structured frame: naming a time period, drawing nature and people together, then articulating the connection in two sentences. A student who fills all three parts has met the task. The drawing and the sentences should be consistent with each other.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawing shows specific, recognisable nature detail (e.g., bare trees, flooded fields, dry sky) AND a human activity clearly linked to it (e.g., farmers planting, children in heavy clothes); sentences name the connection explicitly. Weak: drawing shows generic scenes unconnected to a time period; sentences describe the drawing without explaining the nature–human link.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to draw may write a detailed description instead of a picture. Students who find writing difficult may add labels to their drawing as an alternative to sentences. Both alternative pathways demonstrate the same implied outcome.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled drawing with two written sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the primary creative mode named in C-6.2 and is the mode used in the Seasons' Chart Step 4 story activity; the two sentences ensure the connection is articulated, not merely implied.

assessment_items.question_text: In India, the six seasons are called Ritu. Which of the following correctly names the season that comes after Grishma (summer) in India's classical Ritu system?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. In India's six-Ritu cycle, Varsha (monsoon) follows Grishma (summer). This tests recall of the sequential Ritu names introduced in the 'Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)' section.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Changes Around Us in a Year (Seasons)
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify India's seasonal cycle, name the seasons in their regional and classical traditions, and explain how the same season varies across different regions.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused Shishir (pre-winter/late winter) with the season following summer — possibly listing the Ritu names in the wrong order or guessing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student places Vasanta (spring) after summer, reversing the cycle — they may know the names but not the sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has placed Hemant (pre-winter) after summer, skipping several seasons — suggesting they recall some Ritu names but have not internalised the sequential pattern.

assessment_items.question_text: Name one festival celebrated in winter and one festival celebrated around the spring or new-year harvest season in India. For each festival, write one sentence explaining how that season's nature — what is happening with crops or weather — is connected to why the festival is celebrated at that time.
expected_elements: Names a specific winter festival (e.g., Pongal, Makar Sankranti) with a sentence connecting winter conditions or harvest to the festival.
Names a spring or new-year/harvest festival (e.g., Baisakhi, Gudi Padwa, Vishu, Rongali Bihu, Holi) with a sentence connecting the season's nature to the celebration.
Each sentence shows a clear link between what is happening in nature or agriculture and the reason for the festival at that time.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any festivals named in the 'Celebrating Seasons' section or locally known equivalents. Regional variation is expected — a student from Tamil Nadu may name Pongal for winter and a student from Punjab may name Baisakhi for spring/harvest; both are correct. The key criterion is that the nature–festival connection is articulated, not just the festival name.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between seasonal cycles and cultural practices — crops grown, festivals celebrated, and songs sung — in their own region.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Names a specific winter festival (e.g., Pongal, Makar Sankranti) with a sentence connecting winter conditions or harvest to the festival.
Names a spring or new-year/harvest festival (e.g., Baisakhi, Gudi Padwa, Vishu, Rongali Bihu, Holi) with a sentence connecting the season's nature to the celebration.
Each sentence shows a clear link between what is happening in nature or agriculture and the reason for the festival at that time.

assessment_items.question_text: A friend says: 'Winter is the same everywhere in India — it is cold and people wear heavy clothes.' Do you agree? Using what you know about winter in Kerala compared to Kashmir valley, write a paragraph explaining why winter can feel very different in different parts of India, and why this difference matters for how people live.
look_for: Disagrees with the friend's claim and states that winter varies significantly across India.
Gives a specific contrast between winter in Kerala (mild, near-sea, lower elevation) and winter in Kashmir valley (cold, mountainous, snow possible) using geographical reasoning.
Connects the seasonal difference to how people's lives differ — crops grown, clothes worn, activities possible.
Articulates that geographical features (closeness to sea, mountains, latitude) produce the difference, not just vague regional identity.
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit progressively: responses that name the contrast and a geographical reason score well; responses that also connect to livelihoods and human life score at the top. Accept student phrasing that approximates geographical reasoning even if technical terms are not used.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how geographical differences across regions produce variation in the experience of the same season, and can reflect on the value of seasonal diversity.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

look_for: Disagrees with the friend's claim and states that winter varies significantly across India.
Gives a specific contrast between winter in Kerala (mild, near-sea, lower elevation) and winter in Kashmir valley (cold, mountainous, snow possible) using geographical reasoning.
Connects the seasonal difference to how people's lives differ — crops grown, clothes worn, activities possible.
Articulates that geographical features (closeness to sea, mountains, latitude) produce the difference, not just vague regional identity.

assessment_items.task: Think about the three seasons you know best from where you live — Summer, Monsoon, and Winter. Fill in the table below for each season, then draw a small picture beside each row showing one thing you see in nature during that season.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Season | What I eat | What I wear | A festival or event | What nature looks like (draw here)
Summer | | | |
Monsoon | | | |
Winter | | | |
format_of_output: Completed table with food, clothing, festival, and nature observation for Summer, Monsoon, and Winter
A small drawing for each of the three seasons showing a nature detail
assessment_items.annotation: All answers are region-specific and family-specific — there is no single correct set of foods, clothes, or festivals. Evaluate whether the student's entries are internally consistent (the food, clothes, and festival plausibly belong to the same season) and whether the nature drawings reflect the season described. Regional diversity in responses is expected and should be treated as a strength, not an error.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present their personal and regional experience of seasons through multiple creative modes — written local names, a completed observation table, and a comparative drawing.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can draw on personal and regional experience to populate a structured observation table and represent seasonal nature through drawing, demonstrating that seasons are understood as lived, varied, and culturally embedded — not abstract labels.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The table provides three rows (Summer, Monsoon, Winter) and four columns (food, clothing, festival/event, nature drawing). A complete response fills all twelve cells and adds a small drawing in the nature column for each row. The drawings need not be elaborate — a cloud with rain for monsoon or a bare tree for winter is sufficient.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: entries are specific (a named dish, a named garment or type, a named festival), internally consistent within each season row, and the drawings reflect the season described. Weak: entries are generic ('eat food', 'wear clothes') with no seasonal specificity, or the drawings do not correspond to the season labelled.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write a one-word description in the nature drawing cell instead (e.g., 'hot sun', 'heavy rain', 'bare trees'). Students who find writing difficult may dictate their entries to a peer or the teacher while drawing their nature scenes.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The table format directly mirrors the 'Let us reflect' task in the Celebrating Seasons section (Textbook p. 160), and drawing is an explicitly named mode in C-6.2. The combination ensures both written and visual expression are assessed together.
